title: Rc<T> and RefCell<T>
summary: Shared ownership with reference counting, Rc::clone and strong_count, interior mutability with RefCell and run-time borrow checking, the mock object example, Cell for Copy values, and combining Rc<RefCell<T>> for shared mutable data.

sections: TRPL 15.4 Rc<T>, the Reference Counted Smart Pointer

TRPL 15.5 Allowing Multiple Owners of Mutable Data
PR ch4 Rc and Arc: Shared Ownership

blocks.md:
Ownership usually has one owner. Sometimes a value really has several: in a graph, a node may be pointed to by many edges and should live as long as any of them. **`Rc<T>`** (reference counted) allows that. It keeps a count of how many `Rc`s point to the value and drops the value when the count reaches zero.

*The Rust Programming Language*'s picture: a TV in a family room. The first person in turns it on; others come and watch; the last one to leave turns it off. `Rc<T>` is for **single-threaded** code; chapter 16 has `Arc<T>` for threads.

blocks.title: Sharing a list
blocks.md: Two lists `b` and `c` should share the tail `a`. With `Box`, the first `Cons` would **move** `a` and the second could not use it. With `Rc`, both hold a counted pointer:

blocks.output:
count after creating a = 1
count after creating b = 2
count after creating c = 3
count after c goes out of scope = 2
blocks.explain: `Rc::clone(&a)` does not copy the list; it increments the count and returns another pointer. Writing `Rc::clone(&a)` rather than `a.clone()` is the convention, so deep clones and cheap count bumps look different when reading code.

blocks.caption: `b` and `c` each start with their own `Cons`, then point to the shared list `a`. The count on `a`'s allocation is 3 while all three exist.

blocks.title: Rc gives shared, read-only access
blocks.md: Through an `Rc<T>` you get only `&T`. If several owners could mutate the value, the borrowing rules (one writer or many readers) would be broken. To mutate shared data, combine `Rc` with a type that provides **interior mutability**.

blocks.title: Interior mutability and RefCell<T>
blocks.md:
**Interior mutability** is a design pattern that lets you mutate data even through a shared reference. It is safe because the borrowing rules are still enforced, just at **run time** instead of compile time. **`RefCell<T>`** does this:

- `.borrow()` returns a `Ref<T>`, which acts like `&T`;
- `.borrow_mut()` returns a `RefMut<T>`, which acts like `&mut T`.

`RefCell` counts the active borrows. Asking for `borrow_mut` while any other borrow is alive, or for `borrow` while a mutable one is alive, **panics**. The rules are the same; the check moved from the compiler to the program.

blocks.title: A use case: mock objects

blocks.output: ["Warning: You've used up over 75% of your quota!", "Urgent warning: You've used up over 90% of your quota!"]

thread 'main' panicked at src/main.rs:6:23:
RefCell already borrowed
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
blocks.explain: This compiles, but it breaks the rules at run time, so it panics. `try_borrow_mut()` returns a `Result` instead, for code that wants to handle the conflict.

blocks.title: Cell<T> for small Copy values
blocks.md: `Cell<T>` is a lighter form of interior mutability for `Copy` types: `get()` copies the value out and `set(v)` replaces it. No references to the inside are ever handed out, so no borrow tracking is needed. *Programming Rust* uses it for counters, such as a hit counter on a struct shared by `&`.

blocks.title: Rc<RefCell<T>>: shared and mutable
blocks.md: Combine the two: `Rc` for several owners, `RefCell` for mutation. Every owner can then change the value, and every owner sees the change:

blocks.output:
a after = Cons(RefCell { value: 15 }, Nil)
b after = Cons(RefCell { value: 3 }, Cons(RefCell { value: 15 }, Nil))
c after = Cons(RefCell { value: 4 }, Cons(RefCell { value: 15 }, Nil))
blocks.explain: `value.borrow_mut()` goes through the `Rc` with deref coercion and asks the `RefCell` for a mutable borrow, which ends at the semicolon.

blocks.title: A shared bank account
blocks.md: Two cards share one account. Make `Card` hold an `Rc<RefCell<Account>>` so a payment with either card changes the same balance, and print how many owners the account has.
hints: `self.account.borrow_mut().balance -= amount;` works with `&self`: that is interior mutability.

blocks.title: Shared inventory with mock notifications
blocks.goal: Share mutable state with Rc<RefCell<T>> and test through a trait with a RefCell-based mock.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub trait Notifier { fn notify(&self, msg: &str); }`.
- `pub struct Store { stock: Rc<RefCell<HashMap<String, u32>>>, notifier: Rc<dyn Notifier> }`. Several `Store` values (branches) may share one stock map.
- `pub fn new(stock: &Rc<RefCell<HashMap<String, u32>>>, notifier: Rc<dyn Notifier>) -> Store`.
- `pub fn restock(&self, item: &str, n: u32)` adds to the shared stock.
- `pub fn sell(&self, item: &str, n: u32) -> Result<(), String>`: fails with `"not enough <item>"` (and changes nothing) if stock is too low; on success, if the remaining stock is below 3, calls `notify("low stock: <item> (<left>)")`.
- `pub struct Recorder { pub messages: RefCell<Vec<String>> }` implementing `Notifier` by recording messages, and `pub fn recorder() -> Rc<Recorder>`.

examples.output: Ok(()) and one message "low stock: pen (2)"

hints: In `sell`, take one `borrow_mut()` into a variable, check and update, then **drop** that borrow before calling `notify` (keep the borrow inside a block). The notifier may not need the stock, but holding borrows across calls is a classic source of `already borrowed` panics.
`Rc<Recorder>` coerces to `Rc<dyn Notifier>` when you pass `rec.clone()` where `Rc<dyn Notifier>` is expected.
blocks.solution_explain: `Store`'s methods take `&self`, yet change the shared map: interior mutability. The block in `sell` ends the `borrow_mut` before `notify` runs. `Rc<dyn Notifier>` is a trait object (chapter 18) so the store works with any notifier; the test's `Recorder` is a mock like the one in the lesson.

options: Increments the reference count and returns a new pointer to the same data

questions.q: When is the value inside an Rc dropped?
options: When the first Rc is dropped
When the strong count reaches zero
questions.explanation: The last owner turns off the TV.

questions.q: Why can't you mutate through an `Rc<T>` directly?
options: Several owners with mutable access would break the borrowing rules

questions.q: What happens if you call `borrow_mut()` on a RefCell that is already mutably borrowed?
questions.explanation: The checks happen at run time.

questions.q: Which would you use for a shared counter of type `u32` that you increment through `&self`?
questions.explanation: Cell is ideal for small Copy values.

questions.q: Rc<T> can be sent to another thread.
questions.explanation: Its counter is not thread-safe; use Arc<T>.

points: `Rc<T>` gives several owners shared, read-only access; the value is dropped when the last owner goes.
Interior mutability: `RefCell<T>` allows mutation through `&` and checks the borrowing rules at run time, panicking on violation.
`Cell<T>` is the light version for `Copy` values.
`Rc<RefCell<T>>` is the standard way to have shared mutable data in single-threaded code.

terms.def: A reference-counted smart pointer allowing several owners of the same heap value (single-threaded).
Tracking how many owners a value has and freeing it when the count reaches zero.
A pattern that allows mutating data through shared references, with the rules checked at run time.
A type providing interior mutability by tracking borrows at run time.
Interior mutability for Copy values through get and set, without references.
A stand-in for a real dependency in tests that records how it was used.
